item.title: Beyond the Robot Demo
item.description: NVIDIA’s integrated robotics stack, Eka’s force-aware handling, and Schaeffler’s humanoid component factory tackle the gap between robot demonstrations and useful production. Plus: AMD’s faster simulated decision-making and a palletizing safety zone that moves with the arm.
item.content:encoded:
What turns a capable robot into a useful production system? This week on Physical AI Weekly, Sarah and Daniel examine advances in integration, contact sensing, computation, and safety—and the operating evidence still missing from the announcements.

In this episode

  • NVIDIA connects the stack: Updated Isaac tools link simulation, learning, and onboard execution, while more than 2,000 simulation-ready assets could reduce environment preparation. Shorter setup times remain a vendor claim, and the associated research humanoid platform is scheduled for early 2027—not deployed in a factory.
  • Eka bets on force feedback: A $150 million Series A backs manipulation that combines vision with contact sensing. The company claims 1,500 handling operations per hour, but sustained customer performance, damage rates, and operating costs remain undisclosed.
  • Schaeffler puts humanoids to work: Six humanoids across five stations assemble joint modules at its newly opened Taicang facility. Production monitoring and training could create a useful feedback loop, but output, uptime, intervention rates, and payback have not been published.
  • AMD cuts simulated inference time: Published optimizations reduce model computation from roughly 223 milliseconds to nine on an AMD GPU, with similar reported simulation success. The roughly 25-fold gain is against unoptimized execution—not a measured improvement in physical robot cycle time.
  • beRobox moves the safety zone: An arm-mounted Sonair ultrasonic sensor is intended to let palletizing continue at one station while an operator changes the other pallet. The demonstration does not establish measured throughput gains, and sensor certification does not replace complete-cell safety validation.

The common test is sustained useful output after failed grasps, interventions, maintenance, and safety stops. Better building blocks matter, but their value depends on how reliably—and economically—the whole system works together.

What we're watching

  • Schaeffler’s production results: Component output and human intervention rates would help establish whether the Taicang approach is repeatable.
  • AMD beyond simulation: Independent testing on physical industrial arms, against optimized alternatives, would clarify whether faster computation delivers practical operating gains.

item.title: Intelligence Is Not Throughput
item.description: New robot benchmarks expose the time and cost of turning reasoning into action, while Symbotic, Ubitium and Waymo pursue different paths toward practical deployment. We examine what separates technical capability from reliable, economically useful work.
item.content:encoded:
This week on Physical AI Weekly, Sarah and Daniel examine the gap between intelligent machines and productive systems—from slow robot agents to warehouse integration, prototype chips and driverless rides.

In this episode

  • Robot intelligence meets the clock: Artificial Analysis reports roughly 30 minutes and $16.36 in inference cost per task for its leading robot-arm agent. Separate Vals AI tests highlight the difficulty of building humanoid controllers from scratch—not a verdict on production robots using specialized motor skills.
  • Symbotic buys better handoffs: The acquisition of cellumation adds programmable package-routing technology to Symbotic’s warehouse systems. Simpler layouts and higher throughput are the promise; measured savings and integration results remain to be established.
  • Ubitium’s integrated computing bet: A $14 million funding round supports a chip architecture designed to combine sensing, AI inference and real-time control. First silicon is a proof of concept, with commercial evaluation units planned for 2027 and performance still awaiting independent validation.
  • Waymo opens the enrollment gate: Anyone can now book autonomous rides in San Antonio, San Diego and Tampa—existing operating markets, not three new city launches. Broader access tests demand and operating capacity, but does not establish profitability.

A benchmark, an acquisition, a prototype and a live service offer different kinds of evidence. The common test is useful work delivered reliably at an acceptable total cost.

What we're watching

  • Robot evaluations that support purchasing decisions: Repeated trials reporting completion, elapsed time, interventions and cost together.
  • Warehouse integration results: Symbotic’s integration timetable, throughput per square meter, installed cost and maintenance requirements.
